title: Ezekiel 38:10–16
context: Ezekiel 38:10–16 continues the LORD’s words to Gog through the prophet. Gog devises an evil plan to go up against a land of unwalled villages and plunder a people gathered from the nations who dwell “in the middle of the earth” (38:10–12; compare 5:5, “I have set her in the middle of the nations”). Sheba, Dedan, and the merchants of Tarshish ask whether he has come to take plunder (38:13); Sheba and Dedan are listed among the descendants of Cush in Genesis 10:7, and Tarshish among those of Javan in Genesis 10:4, and they are commonly taken as trading peoples to the south and west, though exact locations are debated. Gog comes from the uttermost parts of the north with a great army (38:15; compare Jeremiah 6:22). The LORD says, “It will happen in the latter days that I will bring you against my land, that the nations may know me when I am sanctified in you, Gog, before their eyes.” (38:16). The oracle thus sets Gog’s own evil intent and the LORD’s purpose side by side. The aim of the passage is the LORD’s self-revelation to the nations, and both traditions read that purpose as shared ground.

verses.text: “ ‘The Lord GOD says: “It will happen in that day that things will come into your mind, and you will devise an evil plan.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says that in that day things will come into Gog’s mind, and he will devise an evil plan. Arminian readers note that Gog’s plan is described as his own evil intent, and they see the oracle holding Gog responsible for the designs he forms against God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same responsibility and read it alongside 38:4 and 38:16, where God brings Gog. They observe that the passage holds God’s purpose and Gog’s evil intent together without explaining how they relate, a point both traditions affirm in their own ways.

verses.text: You will say, ‘I will go up to the land of unwalled villages. I will go to those who are at rest, who dwell securely, all of them dwelling without walls, and having neither bars nor gates,
verses.arminianNotes: Gog says, “I will go up to the land of unwalled villages”, to people at rest who dwell securely. Arminian readers note that Gog sees the people’s security as weakness, and they see the irony that the people’s safety rests not on walls but on God’s protection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same irony and read the unwalled villages as a picture of the peace God has given his restored people. They observe that Gog’s plan misjudges where the people’s real security lies, and both traditions treat the verse as shared ground.

verses.text: to take the plunder and to take prey; to turn your hand against the waste places that are inhabited, and against the people who are gathered out of the nations, who have gotten livestock and goods, who dwell in the middle of the earth.’
verses.arminianNotes: Gog plans to take plunder from a people gathered from the nations, who dwell in the middle of the earth. Arminian readers note the echo of 5:5, “I have set her in the middle of the nations”, and they see God’s people at the center of his purposes for the world.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and read the phrase middle of the earth as describing the people’s central place in God’s plan. They observe that the phrase may also suggest a navel or high point, though the sense is debated, and they hold it loosely.

verses.text: Sheba, Dedan, and the merchants of Tarshish, with all its young lions, will ask you, ‘Have you come to take the plunder? Have you assembled your company to take the prey, to carry away silver and gold, to take away livestock and goods, to take great plunder?’ ” ’
verses.arminianNotes: Sheba, Dedan, and the merchants of Tarshish ask Gog whether he has come to take plunder. Arminian readers note that these trading peoples appear in Genesis 10:4 and 10:7, and they see them as observers interested in the spoils, whose exact locations are debated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same identifications and hold them loosely. They read the merchants’ question as showing that Gog’s invasion is driven by greed, and they observe that the young lions may refer to rulers or warriors, though the sense of the phrase is uncertain.

verses.text: “Therefore, son of man, prophesy, and tell Gog, ‘The Lord GOD says: “In that day when my people Israel dwells securely, will you not know it?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the prophet to say to Gog that in that day, when Israel dwells securely, he will know it. Arminian readers note that the people’s security draws Gog’s attention, and they see in the verse God’s foreknowledge of Gog’s plans and his control over the timing of events.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same awareness and read it as part of God’s sovereign direction of the conflict. They observe that the phrase my people Israel stresses the covenant relationship, and both traditions read the verse as shared ground on God’s care for his restored people.

verses.text: You will come from your place out of the uttermost parts of the north, you, and many peoples with you, all of them riding on horses, a great company and a mighty army.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Gog will come from the uttermost parts of the north with many peoples on horses. Arminian readers note the echo of earlier prophecies of a foe from the north, such as Jeremiah 6:22, named without harmonizing, and they see the north as a symbol of distant threat.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and observe that the north often represents danger in the prophets. They hold the geography loosely and read the verse as describing a vast and distant enemy, a point both traditions treat as shared ground.

verses.text: You will come up against my people Israel as a cloud to cover the land. It will happen in the latter days that I will bring you against my land, that the nations may know me when I am sanctified in you, Gog, before their eyes.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “It will happen in the latter days that I will bring you against my land, that the nations may know me when I am sanctified in you, Gog, before their eyes.” Arminian readers note that God’s purpose is the nations’ knowledge of him, and they see it as aiming at the nations’ recognition of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same purpose and read it as God’s sovereign direction of Gog’s coming for his own glory. They observe that the verse holds God’s purpose and Gog’s intent together, and both traditions treat the knowledge of God among the nations as shared ground.
